scenes.narration: Thirty-five dollars. That is the typical overdraft fee at America's largest banks, according to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. You can pay it for spending just a few dollars more than you have.

Banks have cut these fees sharply in the last few years. Even so, in twenty twenty-three, banks with more than a billion dollars in assets still collected five point eight three billion dollars in overdraft and bounced-payment fees.
So why is a fee that everyone seems to hate still worth billions? And who is really paying it?
By the end of this video, you will know how an overdraft fee is made, why a small group of customers pays most of it, and how a federal cap on the fee was written and then erased.

scenes.narration: Here is what an overdraft is. You have twenty dollars in your checking account. You buy something for twenty-five. The bank can refuse the payment, or it can pay it anyway and push your balance below zero. If it pays, it usually charges you a fee for doing it.

According to the bureau, the median overdraft fee at the largest institutions that charge one was thirty-five dollars. The fee for a payment the bank refuses, called a non-sufficient funds fee, was thirty-two dollars. And the bureau found that the median debit card purchase that triggered an overdraft was only twenty-four dollars.

Think about what that means. The bank covers a twenty-four dollar purchase for a few days, until your next deposit arrives. And it charges thirty-five dollars for the favor. If you called that a short loan, it would be a very expensive one.

And the fees can stack. Wells Fargo, for example, still charges thirty-five dollars per item, up to three times a day. Three small purchases on a bad day can mean one hundred and five dollars in fees.

Let me draw a bad day. Start at ten dollars. A coffee, and the balance is still positive. A grocery run, and it drops below zero. A fee. A gas station, another fee. A streaming bill, a third fee. The purchases add up to less than the fees.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: So who actually ends up paying all these fees? The answer is surprisingly concentrated.

keyframes.label: So who pays all these fees?

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Most people rarely overdraft, or never do. The bureau studied millions of checking accounts. It found that about nine percent of accounts paid almost seventy-nine percent of all overdraft and bounced-payment fees.

It gets even more extreme at the top. Accounts that overdrafted more than twenty times a year were fewer than one in twenty. Yet they paid about sixty-three percent of all those fees. For the bank, the overdraft business does not depend on everyone. It depends on a small group of repeat customers.

keyframes.cue: It depends on a small group
keyframes.label: items[2].at.cue

scenes.narration: Think about who overdraws on a twenty-four dollar purchase. Usually not someone with a large balance. More often, someone waiting for the next paycheck. That is why critics say the fee falls hardest on those who can least afford it.

Some practices made it worse. The bureau described how some banks processed the largest payment of the day first. Paying the big bill first could empty the account faster, so that several small purchases each triggered their own fee.

Regulators also went after something stranger. A purchase was approved when the account had enough money, but by the time it settled, the balance had dropped, and the bank charged an overdraft fee anyway. The bureau called these fees likely unfair. Its examiners found at least tens of millions of dollars in harm, and refunds went to more than one hundred and seventy thousand customers.

Let me draw who pays. Here are one hundred checking accounts. Most of them, ninety-one, pay little or nothing. Nine accounts are on the other side. And those nine pay almost four out of every five fee dollars.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: For years, that model was very profitable. Then, almost overnight, the biggest banks started backing away from it.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: The first crack came years earlier. In twenty ten, a Federal Reserve rule took effect. Banks could no longer charge overdraft fees on ATM withdrawals or one-time debit card purchases unless the customer had opted in. Customers had to say yes first. It was the first time the default had changed.

The bigger shift came at the end of twenty twenty-one. Capital One announced it would stop charging overdraft and bounced-payment fees altogether. Weeks later, Wells Fargo dropped its bounced-payment fee and added a grace period of twenty-four hours, though it kept the overdraft fee itself.

In February twenty twenty-two, Citi said it would end overdraft fees completely, and called itself the only top five American bank to do so. Chase added a fifty-dollar cushion before any fee. And Bank of America reported that its service charges fell by one point one billion dollars in one year, mainly because of its new overdraft policies.

Across the industry, the drop was huge. The bureau counted overdraft and bounced-payment revenue at banks with more than a billion dollars in assets. It was eleven point nine six billion dollars in twenty nineteen. By twenty twenty-three, it was five point eight three billion dollars, down fifty-one percent. The bureau estimated that the average overdrafting household saved about one hundred and eighty-five dollars a year.

Let me draw the drop. Here is twenty nineteen, a tall bar, almost twelve billion dollars. Here is twenty twenty-three, less than half as tall. The banks gave up more than six billion dollars a year. But look at what is left. Almost six billion dollars a year is still a very big business.

scenes.narration: So regulators decided to go further. And for a few months, it looked like the thirty-five dollar fee might disappear.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: In December twenty twenty-four, the bureau issued a final rule for banks and credit unions with more than ten billion dollars in assets. They would have three choices. Charge an overdraft fee of no more than five dollars. Charge a fee that only covered their own costs and losses. Or treat the overdraft as a loan, under the federal lending law, with the disclosures that come with credit.

The bureau projected that the rule could save consumers up to five billion dollars a year, or about two hundred and twenty-five dollars for each household that pays overdraft fees. It was due to take effect in October twenty twenty-five. Wells Fargo warned its investors that it would expect a significant reduction in its overdraft fees.

It never took effect. In twenty twenty-five, Congress used a law called the Congressional Review Act to cancel it. The Senate voted in March. The House voted two hundred and seventeen to two hundred and eleven in April.

And on May ninth, twenty twenty-five, the resolution became law. Its text is very short. The rule, it says, shall have no force or effect. The five-dollar option was gone before a single bank had to offer it.

Let me draw the timeline. December twenty twenty-four, the rule is written. October twenty twenty-five, the rule was supposed to start. But in between, in May twenty twenty-five, Congress erases it. The fee cap lived for five months, only on paper.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: So with no federal cap, what happened to the fees next?

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: The bureau has not published a new total since twenty twenty-three. But outside researchers read the same bank reports. The consulting firm Bates White estimates that banks with more than a billion dollars in assets collected about six point one billion dollars in twenty twenty-four, about three percent more than the year before. In its words, the steep decline appears to have ended.

The money is concentrated at the top. The Consumer Federation of America, an advocacy group, counted four point eight eight billion dollars in twenty twenty-four at banks with more than ten billion dollars in assets. JPMorgan Chase alone took about one billion. Wells Fargo was close behind.

And those numbers leave out a lot. Credit unions and smaller banks do not appear in them. Counting everyone, the National Consumer Law Center cites an estimate of about twelve point one billion dollars in overdraft and bounced-payment fees in twenty twenty-four. That is an estimate, and it measures a much wider group than the bureau did.

Why does the fee survive? Look at how it is built. It is a flat fee. At a bank like Wells Fargo, it is the same thirty-five dollars whether you overdraw by two dollars or by two hundred. On a small purchase, covered for a few days until the next deposit, that is a very wide margin. And without a federal cap, each bank still decides for itself what to charge.

Let me draw the overdraft machine. On the left, a customer close to zero. In the middle, the bank paying a small purchase. On the right, the fee, coming back the moment the paycheck lands. Then the next month, the same customer, the same loop.

So why do banks still make billions from overdrafts? Because the fee is small for most people and huge for a few. It is charged on tiny purchases, paid by customers who live close to zero, and repeated month after month. Banks cut it in half when the pressure was high. The cap that would have cut it again was erased. If you want to keep your money out of that machine, the simplest move is to check whether you opted in.
